statement: If as many numbers as we please beginning from an unit be in continued proportion, and the number after the unit be prime, the greatest will not be measured by any except those which have a place among the proportional numbers.
heath_proof: Let there be as many numbers as we please, A, B, C, D, beginning from an unit and in continued proportion, and let A, the number after the unit, be prime; I say that D, the greatest of them, will not be measured by any other number except A, B, C. For, if possible, let it be measured by E, and let E not be the same with any of the numbers A, B, C. It is then manifest that E is not prime. For, if E is prime and measures D, it will also measure A [IX. 12], which is prime, though it is not the same with it: which is impossible. Therefore E is not prime. Therefore it is composite. But any composite number is measured by some prime number; [VII. 31] therefore E is measured by some prime number. I say next that it will not be measured by any other prime except A. For, if E is measured by another, and E measures D, that other will also measure D; so that it will also measure A [IX. 12], which is prime, though it is not the same with it: which is impossible. Therefore A measures E. And, since E measures D, let it measure it according to F. I say that F is not the same with any of the numbers A, B, C. For, if F is the same with one of the numbers A, B, C, and measures D according to E, therefore one of the numbers A, B, C also measures D according to E. But one of the numbers A, B, C measures D according to some one of the numbers A, B, C; [IX. 11] therefore E is also the same with one of the numbers A, B, C: which is contrary to the hypothesis. Therefore F is not the same as any one of the numbers A, B, C. Similarly we can prove that F is measured by A, by proving again that F is not prime. For, if it is, and measures D, it will also measure A [IX. 12], which is prime, though it is not the same with it: which is impossible; therefore F is not prime. Therefore it is composite. But any composite number is measured by some prime number; [VII. 31] therefore F is measured by some prime number. I say next that it will not be measured by any other prime except A. For, if any other prime number measures F, and F measures D, that other will also measure D; so that it will also measure A [IX. 12], which is prime, though it is not the same with it: which is impossible. Therefore A measures F. And, since E measures D according to F, therefore E by multiplying F has made D. But, further, A has also by multiplying C made D; [IX. 11] therefore the product of A, C is equal to the product of E, F. Therefore, proportionally, as A is to E, so is F to C. [VII. 19] But A measures E; therefore F also measures C. Let it measure it according to G. Similarly, then, we can prove that G is not the same with any of the numbers A, B, and that it is measured by A. And, since F measures C according to G therefore F by multiplying G has made C. But, further, A has also by multiplying B made C; [IX. 11] therefore the product of A, B is equal to the product of F, G. Therefore, proportionally, as A is to F, so is G to B. [VII. 19] But A measures F; therefore G also measures B. Let it measure it according to H. Similarly then we can prove that H is not the same with A. And, since G measures B according to H, therefore G by multiplying H has made B. But further A has also by multiplying itself made B; [IX. 8] therefore the product of H, G is equal to the square on A. Therefore, as H is to A, so is A to G. [VII. 19] But A measures G; therefore H also measures A, which is prime, though it is not the same with it: which is absurd. Therefore D the greatest will not be measured by any other number except A, B, C.
ai_proof_text:
9.13
**Statement:** If as many numbers as we please beginning from an unit be in continued proportion, and the number after the unit be prime, the greatest will not be measured by any except those which have a place among the proportional numbers.

**Step 1.** Let the unit, A, B, C, D be as many numbers as we please beginning from the unit and in continued proportion, so that, as the unit is to A, so is A to B, B to C, and C to D; and let A, the number after the unit, be prime. I say that D, the greatest, is not measured by any number other than the unit, A, B, C, D. For suppose, if possible, that D is measured by a number E which is not the unit and is not the same with any of A, B, C, D.

**Step 2.** Since, as the unit is to A, so is C to D, the unit is the same part of A that C is of D [D7.20]. Now the unit measures A according to the units in A, A being a multitude composed of units [D7.2]; therefore C measures D according to the units in A, that is, D is C added to itself as many times as there are units in A; thus A by multiplying C makes D [D7.15]. In the same way, since, as the unit is to A, so is B to C, A by multiplying B makes C; and since, as the unit is to A, so is A to B, A by multiplying itself makes B. Consequently A measures B, B measures C, and C measures D [D7.15].

**Step 3.** I show first that every number, other than the unit, which measures D is measured by A. Let X be any such number. X is either prime or composite [D7.11, D7.13]. If X is prime, let P be X itself; if X is composite, let P be a prime number which measures X [7.31]. In either case the prime number P measures X, and X measures D; therefore P measures D. Now the unit, A, B, C, D are in continued proportion beginning from the unit, and P is a prime number measuring the last of them; therefore P also measures A, the number next to the unit [9.12]. But A is prime, so that it is measured by the unit alone [D7.11]; and P, being a prime number, is not the unit; hence P is the same with A. Therefore A measures X.

**Step 4.** By Step 3, A measures E; and since E is not the same with A, A is a part of E, the less of the greater [D7.3].

**Step 5.** Since E measures D, let E measure D according to the units in F, so that D is E added to itself as many times as there are units in F; thus F by multiplying E makes D [D7.15], and hence also E by multiplying F makes D [7.16]. F is not the unit, for otherwise D would be E itself, whereas E is not the same with D.

**Step 6.** F is not the same with any of A, B, C. For, if F were one of them, then, since E by multiplying F makes D, F would measure D according to the units in E [D7.15]; but F, having a place among the proportional numbers before D, measures D according to some one of the numbers which have a place among the proportional numbers [9.11]; and the number according to which F measures D is one only; hence E would be the same with one of the unit, A, B, C, D, contrary to hypothesis. Therefore F is a number which is not the same with any of the unit, A, B, C.

**Step 7.** Since A by multiplying C makes D (Step 2) and E by multiplying F makes D (Step 5), the product of A, C is equal to the product of E, F; therefore, as A is to E, so is F to C [7.19]. But A is a part of E (Step 4); therefore F is the same part of C [D7.20], so that F measures C. Let F measure C according to the units in G; then G by multiplying F makes C [D7.15], and F by multiplying G makes C [7.16].

**Step 8.** G is not the unit, for otherwise C would be F itself, whereas F is not the same with C (Step 6). Nor is G the same with A or with B: for, if it were, then, since F by multiplying G makes C, G would measure C according to the units in F [D7.15]; but the unit, A, B, C are in continued proportion beginning from the unit, and G, having a place among these proportional numbers before C, measures C according to some one of the numbers which have a place among them [9.11]; hence F would be the same with one of the unit, A, B, C, contrary to Step 6. Therefore G is a number not the same with any of the unit, A, B. Moreover, F measures C and C measures D (Step 2), so that F measures D; therefore A measures F (Step 3), and, F not being the same with A, A is a part of F [D7.3].

**Step 9.** Since A by multiplying B makes C (Step 2) and F by multiplying G makes C (Step 7), the product of A, B is equal to the product of F, G; therefore, as A is to F, so is G to B [7.19]. But A is a part of F (Step 8); therefore G is the same part of B [D7.20], so that G measures B. Let G measure B according to the units in H; then H by multiplying G makes B [D7.15], and G by multiplying H makes B [7.16].

**Step 10.** H is not the unit, for otherwise B would be G itself, whereas G is not the same with B (Step 8). Nor is H the same with A: for, if it were, then, since G by multiplying H makes B, H, that is A, would measure B according to the units in G [D7.15]; but the unit, A, B are in continued proportion beginning from the unit, and A measures B according to some one of the numbers which have a place among these proportional numbers [9.11]; hence G would be the same with one of the unit, A, B, contrary to Step 8. Therefore H is a number which is neither the unit nor A. Moreover, G measures B, B measures C, and C measures D (Step 2), so that G measures D; therefore A measures G (Step 3), and, G not being the same with A, A is a part of G [D7.3].

**Step 11.** Since A by multiplying itself makes B (Step 2) and G by multiplying H makes B (Step 9), the product of A, A is equal to the product of G, H; therefore, as A is to G, so is H to A [7.19]. But A is a part of G (Step 10); therefore H is the same part of A [D7.20], so that H measures A. Thus the prime number A is measured by a number H which is neither the unit nor A itself (Step 10); but a prime number is measured by the unit alone [D7.11]: which is impossible.

**Step 12.** Therefore no such number E exists, and D, the greatest, is not measured by any number except those which have a place among the proportional numbers. If the continued proportion beginning from the unit has more terms, the same descent applies: a supposed measurer of the greatest term which is not among the proportional numbers yields, as in Steps 5 to 7, a measurer of the term before it which again is not among the proportional numbers, and so on until the number next to the unit is reached, where the argument of Step 11 gives the same impossibility. Q.E.D.
